Fear flinches at the strange and the sudden, threats to the things it loves, and scrambles to keep them safe — but to you what is strange? What is sudden? Who can take from you what you love? And where, except with you, is safety that cannot be shaken? Grief pines over lost things its desire once fed on with delight, wishing nothing could ever be taken from it — the way nothing can be taken from you.

This is how the soul commits fornication: it turns away from you and looks outside you for what it can never find pure and unclouded until it comes back to you. All those who put themselves far from you and raise themselves up against you are imitating you — perversely. But even by imitating you that way, they admit that you are the Creator of the whole of nature, and that therefore there is nowhere to withdraw from you altogether. So what did I love in that theft? In what way was I imitating my Lord — even viciously, even perversely? Did it please me to break your law by fraud, since I could not break it by force — to play at a maimed freedom, prisoner that I was, by getting away with what was not allowed, in a shadow-play of omnipotence? Look at him: a slave running from his master, and what he catches is a shadow. What rottenness! What a monstrosity of life, what a depth of death — that I could like a thing I was not allowed to do, for no reason except that I was not allowed!

What can I give back to the Lord for this — that my memory can revisit all of it and my soul feel no terror? I will love you, Lord, and thank you, and confess to your name, because you have forgiven me such evils, such unspeakable acts of mine. I put it down to your grace and your mercy that you melted my sins away like ice. And I put down to your grace, too, all the evil I did not do. What was I not capable of — I, who could love a crime for nothing? I confess it has all been forgiven me: the evils I did by my own choice, and the evils that, with you steering, I did not do. Where is the man who will weigh his own weakness and still dare to credit his purity and innocence to his own strength — and so love you less, as though he had less need of that mercy of yours by which you forgive the sins of everyone who turns to you? A man you called, who followed your voice and kept clear of the things he now reads me remembering and confessing about myself — let him not laugh at me. I was sick, and I was healed by the same Physician who kept him from falling sick, or rather kept him less sick. Let him love you for that as much as I do — no, more: for he sees that the one who pulled me out of so deep a wasting sickness of sin is the very one who kept him from wasting that way at all.

What harvest did I ever get, wretched as I was, from the things I blush now to remember — above all from that theft, in which the theft itself was all I loved? The theft itself was nothing — and I was that much more wretched for loving it. And yet, alone, I would not have done it. I remember what I was then: alone, I would never have done it. So I also loved the company of the ones I did it with. Then I did love something besides the theft after all? No — nothing besides; because the company, too, was nothing. What is it really? Who can teach me, except the one who lights up my heart and clears out its dark corners? What is this thing that has come into my mind to be asked about, argued, weighed? If I had loved the pears I stole, and wanted the taste of them, I could have done it alone — if the wrong itself had been enough to deliver my pleasure. I would not have needed to kindle the itch of my desire against the friction of accomplice minds. But my pleasure was not in those pears. It was in the crime itself, and the crime was made by the company of us sinning together.

What was that state of mind? Whatever it was, it was foul beyond words, and woe to me for having it. But what was it? Who understands his own faults? It was laughter — a kind of tickle in the heart at the thought that we were fooling people who never suspected us and would have hated what we were doing. Why, then, did it delight me that I was not doing it alone? Is it that nobody laughs easily alone? Not easily, no — and yet laughter will sometimes overpower a person who is completely alone, with no one else anywhere near, if something funny enough strikes his senses or his mind. But this — I would not have done this alone. Alone, I would never have done it. Here it is before you, my God: the living memory of my soul. By myself I would not have committed that theft — a theft in which what I stole gave me no pleasure, only the stealing did; and stealing by myself would have given me none, and I would not have stolen. Unfriendly friendship! Seduction of the mind that no one can trace: out of games and jokes, a greed to do harm; an appetite for another's loss, with nothing in it for me — no gain, no grudge. Just someone saying, "Come on — let's do it," and the shame of not being shameless.

Who can untangle that twisted, matted knot? It is foul. I do not want to keep staring at it; I do not want to see it. I want you — Justice, Innocence, beautiful and honorable to honest eyes, a fullness no one ever tires of. With you is rest, rest to the very bottom, and life that nothing disturbs. Whoever enters into you enters into the joy of his Lord; he will not be afraid, and he will be at his best in the One who is best. I drained away from you and I wandered, my God — too far off every path from you, my steadiness, in those years of my youth — and I became to myself a land of famine.

I came to Carthage, and a cauldron of shameful loves hissed and seethed around me. I was not in love yet, but I was in love with loving, and out of a deeper, hidden need I hated myself for not needing more. I hunted for something to love, in love with loving itself; I hated safety, hated a road without traps. For inside me was a famine of the inner food — of you yourself, my God — yet the famine gave me no hunger. I had no appetite for the food that does not spoil, not because I was full of it, but because the emptier I was, the more it turned my stomach. That is why my soul was sick, and broke out in sores, and flung itself wretchedly outward, itching to be scratched by the touch of things of sense. Yet if those things had no soul in them, they would not be loved at all. To love and to be loved was sweet to me, and sweeter if I could also enjoy the body of the one who loved me. So I fouled the spring of friendship with the dirt of lust; I clouded its brightness with a hell of desire; and, foul and disgraceful as I was, in my overflowing vanity I longed to pass for elegant and refined. I fell headlong into the love I was aching to be caught by. My God, my mercy, how much gall you sprinkled over that sweetness — and what goodness it was to do it! For I was loved in return; I came in secret to the bond of enjoying; and I was glad to be tied up in chains of misery, so that I could be flogged with the burning iron rods of jealousy and suspicion, of fear and anger and quarrels.

Stage shows swept me away too, full of images of my own miseries and fuel for my own fire. Why is it that a man in the theater wants to feel grief, watching sorrowful and tragic things he would never willingly suffer himself? Yet as a spectator he wants to suffer grief at them, and the grief itself is his pleasure. What is that but wretched madness? The more a man is stirred by these performances, the less he has recovered from such passions himself — though when he suffers in his own person we call it misery, and when he feels with someone else we call it compassion. But what sort of compassion is there for fictions on a stage? The listener is not being called to help; he is only being invited to grieve, and the more he grieves, the louder he applauds the actor of those fictions. And if these human calamities — ancient ones, or pure inventions — are played so that the spectator feels no sorrow, he walks out disgusted and muttering criticism; but if sorrow is stirred in him, he stays riveted to his seat, weeping for joy.

So griefs are loved too? Surely joy is what everyone wants. Or is it this — that though no one likes to be miserable, we do like to be merciful, and since mercy cannot exist without grief, for this one reason griefs are loved? This too springs from that vein of friendship. But where does it go? Where does it flow? Why does it run down into a torrent of boiling pitch, into those monstrous tides of foul lust into which it is changed and twisted — by its own choice bent and hurled down out of its heavenly clearness? Should compassion be thrown out, then? By no means. Let griefs, then, sometimes be loved. But beware of uncleanness, my soul — with my God for your guardian, the God of our fathers, to be praised and exalted above all forever — beware of uncleanness. Even now I have not stopped pitying. But in those days, in the theaters, I rejoiced with the lovers when they wickedly enjoyed one another, though it was all make-believe in the play; and when they lost one another I grieved with them as if I were deep in compassion — and both delighted me all the same. Now I pity the man who rejoices in his wickedness far more than the man who is thought to have suffered hardship because he missed some ruinous pleasure and lost some miserable happiness. This is surely the truer mercy, but there is no delight in its grief. For though a man who grieves for the wretched is commended for his act of love, the man who is genuinely compassionate would far rather there were nothing to grieve about. Only if goodwill could be ill will — which can never be — could a man who truly and sincerely pities wish for wretched people to exist so that he could pity them. Some sorrow, then, can be approved; none can be loved. For this is your way, Lord God: you love souls far more purely than we do, and pity them more incorruptibly, because no sorrow can wound you. And who is equal to these things?

But I, wretched then, loved to grieve, and went looking for something to grieve over. In another man's misery — faked, staged — the performance I liked best, the one that pulled at me hardest, was the one that shook tears out of me. Was it any wonder that an unhappy sheep, straying from your flock, sick of your keeping, broke out in an ugly mange? That was where my love of griefs came from — not griefs that would cut me deep, since I had no wish to suffer the things I loved to watch, but griefs that, heard and invented, scraped me lightly on the surface. And after them, as after raking fingernails, came the hot swelling, the abscess, the festering sore. That was my life — but was it life, my God?

And your faithful mercy circled over me, far off. On what enormous iniquities I wasted myself! I followed a sacrilegious curiosity, so that, having deserted you, it might drag me down to the treacherous depths, to the cheating service of demons — and to them I sacrificed my evil deeds. And in all of it you were flogging me. I even dared, while your solemn rites were being celebrated inside the walls of your own church, to feel desire, and to set about a piece of business whose fruit was death. For that you lashed me with heavy punishments, but nothing next to my fault, O you, my exceedingly great mercy, my God, my refuge from the terrible destroyers among whom I wandered, stiff-necked, drawing further and further away from you — loving my own ways and not yours, loving a runaway's freedom.

Those studies too, the ones people called honorable, had their eye on the law courts: I was to excel in them, and the more crooked I was, the more I would be praised. So great is the blindness of men, who glory even in their blindness. And I was now the senior student in the rhetoric school, and I rejoiced in it proudly and swelled with conceit — though I was far quieter, Lord, you know it, and stood completely apart from the wrecking done by the "Wreckers." That crooked, devilish name was worn like a badge of sophistication. I lived among them, ashamed with a shameless shame that I was not one of them. I was with them; at times I enjoyed their friendships; but their doings I always abhorred — their "wreckings," the insolent way they hounded the shyness of strangers, tormenting it with unprovoked mockery and feeding their own malicious glee on it. Nothing could be more like the conduct of demons. So what truer name could they have than Wreckers? — wrecked and twisted themselves first, while the lying spirits secretly laughed at them and seduced them in the very thing they loved to do: laughing at others, and deceiving them.

Among such men, at that impressionable age, I studied the books of eloquence, in which I longed to stand out — a damnable and windy purpose, aimed at the joys of human vanity. Following the usual course of study, I came to a book by one Cicero, whose tongue almost everyone admires; his heart, not so much. That book contains his exhortation to philosophy, and it is called the Hortensius. That book changed what I loved. It turned my prayers toward you yourself, Lord, and gave me new purposes, new desires. All at once every vain hope was worthless to me; I longed for the immortality of wisdom with an unbelievable burning of the heart; and I had begun to rise, so that I might return to you. For it was not to sharpen my tongue — the thing I was supposedly buying with my mother's money, in my nineteenth year, my father two years dead — it was not to sharpen my tongue that I took up that book. What had won me was not the way it spoke, but what it said.

How I burned then, my God — how I burned to fly up from earthly things back to you! And I did not know what you were doing with me. For wisdom is with you. The love of wisdom has a Greek name, "philosophy," and that book set me on fire with it. There are men who use philosophy to seduce, coloring and painting over their own errors with that great, smooth, honorable name; and nearly all who did so, in Cicero's day and before it, are marked and exposed in that book. It even makes plain that saving warning of your Spirit, spoken through your good and devout servant: "See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deceit, following human tradition, following the elements of this world and not Christ; for in him the whole fullness of deity dwells in bodily form." And at that time — you know it, light of my heart — those words of the apostle were still unknown to me. What delighted me in Cicero's exhortation was just this: that his words roused me, kindled me, set me ablaze to love and seek and win and hold and strongly embrace not this school or that school, but wisdom itself, whatever it might be. Only one thing dampened the blaze: the name of Christ was not there. For that name, by your mercy, Lord — the name of my Savior, your Son — my tender heart had drunk in devoutly with my mother's milk, and it stayed deep in me; and whatever came without that name, however learned, however polished, however true, could not carry me away entirely.

So I resolved to turn my mind to the holy Scriptures, and see what kind of thing they were. And what I see there is a thing not opened to the proud, not laid bare to children: lowly at the threshold, lofty as you go deeper in, and veiled in mysteries. I was not the kind of man who could enter it, or bend my neck to walk at its pace. When I first turned to Scripture, I did not feel what I am saying now. It seemed to me unworthy to stand beside the stateliness of Cicero. My swollen pride recoiled from its plainness, and my sharp eye could not pierce its depths. Yet Scripture is exactly the thing that grows up with a little child. But I sneered at being a little child; puffed up with self-importance, I took myself for a great man.

And so I fell in with men proudly raving, all flesh and all talk, whose mouths held the devil's snares — a birdlime mixed from the syllables of your name, and of the Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Paraclete, our Comforter, the Holy Spirit. These names never left their mouths, but only as sound, as the noise of the tongue; their hearts were empty of truth. "Truth! Truth!" they kept saying, and they said it to me constantly, and it was nowhere in them. They spoke falsehoods — not only about you, who truly are the Truth, but even about the elements of this world, your creation. Even the philosophers who say true things about such matters I should have passed by, for love of you, my Father, supremely good, beauty of all things beautiful. O Truth, Truth — how the marrow of my soul sighed for you, even then, from the inside, while those men sounded your name at me over and over, in many ways, with the voice alone and with many enormous books! Those books were the platters on which — while I starved for you — they served me the sun and the moon in your place: beautiful works of yours, but works of yours all the same. Not you. Not even your first works: for your spiritual works come before these bodily ones, bright and heavenly though they are. But I was hungry and thirsty not even for those first works, but for you yourself, the Truth, in whom there is no change, no shadow of turning. And still they kept setting glittering fantasies before me on those platters. Better to love this actual sun — real at least to these eyes — than those falsehoods that use the eyes to cheat the mind. And yet, because I took them for you, I ate — not eagerly, since in my mouth you had no taste of what you are (you were not those empty fictions), and I was not nourished by them; I was drained. Food in dreams looks exactly like the food of waking life; yet the sleeping are not fed by it — they are asleep. But those doctrines were not like you in any way, as you have now spoken to me, for they were bodily fantasies — false bodies. More certain than they are these true bodies we see with the sight of the flesh, in the sky or on the earth. The beasts and the birds see them just as we do, and they are more certain than when we picture them in the mind; and again, we picture them with more certainty than when we start from them and guess at other bodies, vaster and infinite, that do not exist at all. Such were the empty husks I was fed on then — and I was not fed. But you, my Love, for whom I grow faint so that I may grow strong — you are neither those bodies we see, though they are in heaven, nor those we do not see there; for you created them, and you do not even count them among your greatest works. How far you are, then, from those fantasies of mine, fantasies of bodies that have no being at all! More certain than those are the images of bodies that do exist, and more certain than the images the bodies themselves — and even they are not you. Nor are you the soul, which is the life of bodies — and the life of bodies is better and more certain than the bodies. No: you are the life of souls, the life of lives, alive by your own self, and you do not change — O life of my soul.

Where were you then, for me? How far away? I was wandering far from you, shut out even from the husks of the pigs whom I was feeding on husks. How much better are the little fables of the poets and the schoolmasters than those traps! Verses, songs, "Medea in flight" — these are truly more useful than those men's five elements, painted up in different disguises to match their five dens of darkness: things that do not exist at all, and that kill whoever believes in them. A verse and a song I can turn into real food. And though I sang of Medea flying, I never claimed it happened; though I heard it sung, I never believed it. But those things I believed. Woe, woe! By what steps was I dragged down into the depths of hell — toiling and seething for lack of the truth! For I was seeking you, my God — to you I confess it, who took pity on me before I could yet confess — I was seeking you not by the understanding of the mind, by which you willed me to stand above the beasts, but by the senses of the flesh. And all the while you were more inward than my inmost part, and higher than my highest. I had walked into that brazen woman of Solomon's riddle, poor in prudence, who sits on a stool at her door and says, "Eat hidden bread gladly, and drink sweet stolen water." She seduced me, because she found me living outside, in the eye of my flesh, chewing over in myself the food I had gulped down through it.

For I did not know that other thing, the one that truly is. And I was subtly nudged — sharp fellow that I was — to side with fools and deceivers when they put their questions to me: Where does evil come from? Is God bounded by a bodily shape — does he have hair and nails? Are men to be counted righteous who had several wives at once, and killed men, and sacrificed animals? In my ignorance these questions shook me, and while I was walking away from the truth I imagined I was walking toward it. For I did not yet know that evil has no being of its own — that it is nothing but the privation of good, thinning down toward the point where nothing at all is left. How could I have seen that, when my eyes' seeing stopped at bodies, and my mind's seeing stopped at a phantasm? And I did not know that God is spirit: not something with limbs stretched out in length and breadth, not something whose being is bulk. For bulk is smaller in its part than in its whole; and if it were infinite, it would be smaller in any part you marked off by a fixed space than in its whole infinity — so it is not whole everywhere, the way spirit is, the way God is. And what there is in us by which we exist, and by which Scripture rightly says we are made in the image of God — of that I was completely ignorant.

Nor did I know the true inner righteousness, which judges not by custom but by the perfectly straight law of almighty God — the law by which the moral codes of regions and ages were shaped to fit those regions and ages, while the law itself is the same always and everywhere, not one thing in one place and something else in another. By that law Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and Moses and David were righteous — all those men praised by the mouth of God himself. It is fools who judge them unrighteous, judging by man's judgment and measuring the moral conduct of the whole human race against the yardstick of their own small habits. It is as if a man in an armory, with no idea what fits which limb, tried to cover his head with a shin-guard and put a helmet on his foot, and then complained that nothing fits. Or as if, on a day when trade is publicly banned after noon, a shopkeeper fumed that he could not sell in the afternoon, since he had been allowed to in the morning. Or as if, in a single house, a man watched one servant handle something the cup-bearer is not allowed to touch, or saw a thing done behind the stables that is forbidden at the dinner table, and grew indignant that in one dwelling, in one household, the same thing is not granted to everyone everywhere. Such are the people who bristle when they hear that something was lawful for righteous men in that age which is not lawful in this one, or that God commanded those men one thing and these men another, for reasons belonging to the times — though both alike were obeying the same righteousness. Yet they can see that in one man, one day, one house, different things fit different members; that a thing lawful for years may cease to be lawful; that something permitted or commanded in one corner is justly forbidden and punished in another. Is justice then fickle and changeable? No. But the times over which justice presides do not run alike — they are times, after all. And men, whose life on earth is short, cannot stitch together by their own experience the circumstances of earlier ages and other nations, which they never knew, with what they know first-hand — though within a single body, a single day, a single household, they can easily see what suits each member, each moment, each part and person. At the one they take offense; to the other they submit.

All this I did not know then, and did not notice. It struck my eyes on every side, and I did not see it. I wrote verses, and in them I was not free to set any foot in any position; each meter demanded something different, and even within one meter the same foot could not stand in every place. Yet the art by which I composed did not have one rule here and a different rule there; it held them all at once. And still I could not see that the righteousness which good and holy men obeyed held everything it commands together in one — far more excellently, far more sublimely — varying in no part of itself, and yet, for varying times, distributing and prescribing not everything at once, but what was proper to each. Blind as I was, I faulted the devout fathers — not only for using the things of their own day as God commanded and inspired them, but also for foretelling what was to come, as God revealed it through them.

Can it ever, anywhere, be unjust to love God with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind — and to love your neighbor as yourself? So the offenses that are against nature are everywhere and always to be detested and punished; such were the offenses of Sodom. If every nation on earth committed them, all would stand guilty of the same crime under God's law, which did not make human beings to use one another so. For the very fellowship that ought to hold between God and us is violated when the nature of which he is the author is defiled by perverted lust. But offenses against the customs of men are to be avoided according to the customs of each place, so that a compact settled among themselves by a city's or a nation's custom or law may not be broken at the whim of anyone, citizen or foreigner. For any part that will not fit its own whole is ugly. When God commands something contrary to the custom or the compact of any people, however, then even if it was never done there, it must be done; if it has lapsed, it must be restored; if it was never instituted, it must be instituted now. For if a king, in the city he rules, may lawfully command what no one before him — nor he himself until then — had ever commanded, and obeying him is no offense against the community of that city (indeed it is an offense not to obey him, since the general compact of human society is to obey its kings), then how much more must God, the ruler of all his creation, be obeyed without hesitation in whatever he commands. For just as, among the powers of human society, the greater authority is set above the lesser and is obeyed first, so God is set above all.

The same holds for acts of violence, where there is an appetite to hurt — by insult or by injury — and either for revenge, as enemy against enemy; or to seize some advantage that belongs to another, as robber against traveler; or to ward off an evil, against someone who is feared; or out of envy, as the wretched envy the fortunate, or a man who has prospered envies the one he fears will pull level with him, or aches to see already level; or for the sheer pleasure of another's pain, like the spectators at the gladiators, or the people who mock and jeer at whomever they please. These are the chief heads of iniquity, and they sprout from the lust to rule, the lust to look, the lust to feel — from one of them, or two, or all three at once. And so men live evil lives against the three and the seven — that harp of ten strings, your Ten Commandments, O God most high, most sweet. But what can foul offenses do to you, who cannot be defiled? What violence can reach you, who cannot be harmed? What you avenge is what men do to themselves; for even when they sin against you, they are doing wicked harm to their own souls. Iniquity lies to itself — whether by corrupting and perverting its own nature, which you made and set in order; or by using permitted things without measure; or by burning for forbidden things, for that use which is against nature; or men stand guilty of raging against you in heart and word, kicking against the goad; or, bursting the fences of human society, they brazenly exult in private alliances and private feuds, as this or that tempts or offends them. And all of it happens when you are forsaken, O fountain of life, the one true creator and ruler of the universe — when private pride fastens its love on one false thing, a mere part of the whole. So the way back to you is a humble devotion: and you cleanse us of our evil habit; you are merciful to the sins of those who confess; you hear the groaning of the shackled, and you loose us from the chains we made for ourselves — if only we stop lifting against you the horns of a false liberty, greedy to have more at the risk of losing everything, and loving our own private good more than you, the good of all things.

And yet among these offenses of foulness and of violence and so many iniquities, there are the sins of people who are making progress. Those who judge rightly fault these sins by the rule of perfection, but praise the persons in hope of the harvest, as one praises the green blade for the grain to come. And there are certain acts that look like foul or violent offenses and are not sins at all, because they offend neither you, our Lord God, nor the bond of society: as when a man gathers things suited to his season of life for its use, and we cannot tell whether a lust for owning drove him; or when established authority punishes in order to correct, and we cannot tell whether a lust for hurting drove it. Many an act, then, that seems blameworthy in men's sight is approved by your testimony, and many an act praised by men is condemned with you as witness — because the look of the deed is one thing, the mind of the doer another, and the hidden hinge of the moment another still. But when you suddenly command something unaccustomed and unforeseen — even a thing you once forbade — and for the time being keep the reason of your command hidden, and it cuts against the compact of some human society, who can doubt that it must be done? — for the only human society that is just is the one that serves you. But blessed are those who know that it is you who command. For everything your servants did was done either to show what the present hour needed, or to foreshadow what was to come.

Ignorant of all this, I laughed at those holy servants and prophets of yours. And what did my laughing accomplish, except that you laughed at me? For little by little, step by step, I was drawn into absurdities like these: that a fig weeps when it is picked, and that its mother the tree sheds tears of milk. And yet if some Manichaean "saint" ate that fig — picked, naturally, by someone else's guilt, not his own — he would blend it into his guts and breathe angels out of it; better still, as he groaned and moaned in prayer, he would belch up particles of God — particles of the most high and true God that would have stayed locked in that fruit forever had they not been freed by the teeth and belly of one of the Elect. And I, wretch that I was, believed that more mercy was owed to the fruits of the earth than to the human beings for whose sake they grow. If a hungry man who was not a Manichee had asked for a bite, giving it to him would have seemed like sentencing that morsel to death.

And you sent down your hand from on high and drew my soul out of that deep darkness — because my mother, your faithful one, wept to you for me, more than mothers weep over the bodies of dead children. By the faith and the spirit she had from you, she saw my death; and you heard her, Lord. You heard her, and did not despise her tears when they streamed down and watered the ground beneath her eyes in every place where she prayed. You heard her. For where else did that dream come from, by which you comforted her, so that she consented to live with me and share the same table in her house? She had begun to refuse it, turning away in loathing from the blasphemies of my error. In the dream she saw herself standing on a kind of wooden rule, and a radiant young man coming toward her, cheerful and smiling at her, while she grieved, crushed under her grief. He asked her the causes of her sorrow and her daily tears — asking, as such visitors do, to teach and not to learn — and she answered that she was mourning my perdition. Then he told her to rest easy, and bade her look and see: where she was, there I was also. And she looked, and saw me standing beside her on the same rule. Where did this come from, if not that your ears were bent to her heart? O good Omnipotent — you who care for each one of us as if you cared for that one alone, and care for all as if for one.

And where did this come from too? When she told me the vision, and I tried to twist it to mean that she should not despair of one day being what I was, she answered at once, without a moment's hesitation: "No. It was not said to me, Where he is, there you will be. It was said, Where you are, there he will be." I confess to you, Lord, as far as I remember — and I have told it often — that this answer of yours through my mother, wide awake, moved me even then more than the dream itself, in which the joy of that devout woman, to be fulfilled so long afterward, was foretold so long in advance to console her present anguish. She was not thrown by my false reading, plausible as it was; she saw in an instant what had to be seen, which I certainly had not seen until she said it. For almost nine years followed, in which I wallowed in the mud of that deep pit and in the darkness of falsehood — often trying to rise, and slammed down all the harder. And through all that time, that chaste, devout, and sober widow — the kind you love — brisker now with hope, but no slacker in weeping and mourning, never stopped lamenting over me to you in every hour of her prayers. Her prayers came into your presence — and still you let me roll, and roll again, in that darkness.

Meanwhile you gave her another answer, one I remember — for I am passing over much, hurrying toward the things that most press me to confess to you, and much I have simply forgotten. You gave her another answer, then, through a priest of yours, a certain bishop reared in the church and well trained in your books. When that woman begged him to be so kind as to talk with me — to refute my errors, unteach me my evils and teach me what was good (he did this whenever he found people fit for it) — he refused, and wisely, as I understood afterwards. He answered that I was still unteachable: I was puffed up with the newness of that heresy, and had already needled plenty of untrained people with my little trick questions, as she herself had told him. "Leave him alone for a while," he said. "Only pray to the Lord for him. Reading on his own, he will discover what that error is, and how great its impiety." At the same time he told her how he himself, as a small boy, had been handed over to the Manichees by his mother, who had been led astray; how he had not only read but copied out nearly all their books; and how it had become plain to him, with no one arguing or persuading him, that the sect was to be fled — and he had fled it. When he had said this and she still would not be satisfied, but pressed him harder, pleading and weeping freely, that he would see me and talk with me, he lost patience a little at her insistence and said: "Go now, leave me. As surely as you live, it cannot be that the son of these tears should be lost." In her talks with me afterward she often recalled that she had received those words as if they had sounded from heaven.

For nine years — from my nineteenth year to my twenty-eighth — we lived seduced and seducing, deceived and deceiving, through one desire after another: openly, by way of the studies they call liberal; secretly, under a false name of religion. Proud on the one side, superstitious on the other, empty everywhere. On the one hand we chased the hollowness of popular glory, right down to applause in the theater, prize poems, contests for garlands of hay, the trash of the shows, the appetites that keep no measure. On the other we wanted to be scrubbed clean of all that filth by carrying food to the people called "elect" and "holy," so that in the workshop of their own stomachs they could manufacture angels and gods for us — the gods who were supposed to set us free. That is what I pursued; that is what I practiced with my friends — friends deceived by me, and deceived along with me. Let the arrogant laugh at me, and all those you have not yet struck down and broken for their own healing, my God: I will still confess my shame to you, and make it your praise. Let me do it, I beg you; give me the grace to walk back, in present memory, around the old loops of my wandering, and to offer you a sacrifice of rejoicing. For what am I to myself, without you, but a guide leading myself off the cliff? And what am I even at my best but a creature suckling your milk, feeding on you, the food that never spoils? And what kind of man is any man, seeing that he is a man? Let the strong and the powerful laugh at us, then. We are weak and poor, and we will confess to you.

In those years I taught rhetoric. Defeated by greed, I sold the kind of speech that wins. Even so — Lord, you know this — I preferred to have good students, as students are reckoned good, and without deceit I taught them deceit: not the kind to be used against an innocent man's life, though sometimes for a guilty man's. And you, God, watching from far off, saw my good faith stagger on that slippery ground and throw off a few sparks through all the smoke — the good faith I kept in teaching men who loved emptiness and went hunting for lies, I their fellow traveler. In those years I had a woman. She was not mine in what is called lawful marriage; a restless passion, empty of prudence, had found her out. But she was the only one, and I kept faith with her bed. And with her I learned firsthand the distance between the covenant of marriage, entered for the sake of children, and the bargain of a lustful love — where a child is born against the parents' wishes, though once born, it makes them love it.

I remember, too, that when I had decided to enter a competition for theatrical verse, some soothsayer sent word to ask what I would pay him to win it. I loathed and detested those filthy rites, and I answered that even if the garland were made of gold that never perishes, I would not let a fly be killed to win it — for he was going to kill living creatures in his sacrifices, and by those honors, it seemed, to recruit demons to back me. But even this evil I refused not out of any pure love for you, God of my heart. I did not know how to love you; I did not know how to conceive of anything beyond material light. And a soul that sighs after fictions like those — isn't it whoring away from you, trusting in shams, feeding the winds? I would not have sacrifices offered to demons on my behalf; yet by my superstition I was offering myself to them all the while. For what else is "feeding the winds" but feeding the demons themselves — becoming, by our straying, their entertainment and their joke?

But those frauds they call astrologers I consulted without a scruple, because they seemed to use no sacrifice and to aim no prayer at any spirit for their divinations. Christian and true devotion rejects that art too, and condemns it — consistently. For it is a good thing to confess to you and to say, Have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you; not to twist your mercy into a license to sin, but to remember the Lord's words: Look, you have been made well. Sin no more, or something worse may happen to you. All that healthy counsel the astrologers labor to kill, telling us, "The cause of your sin is fixed, inescapably, in the sky," and "Venus did this, or Saturn, or Mars" — so that man, this flesh and blood, this proud rot, might carry no blame, while the blame lands on the maker and orderer of heaven and the stars. And who is that but our God — the very sweetness and wellspring of justice, who repays each of us according to our works, and does not despise a broken and contrite heart?

There was in those days a shrewd man, deeply skilled in medicine and famous in it, who as proconsul had set that contest garland, with his own hand, on my head — my sick head, though he did not set it there as a doctor. For that disease you alone cure — you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble. But did you fail me even through that old man? Did you leave off healing my soul? I came to know him better, and I hung steadily, intently, on what he said; the words were plain, but the talk was quick, alive, and serious. When he gathered from my conversation that I was devoted to the books of the horoscope-casters, he advised me — kindly, like a father — to throw them away, and not to waste on that nonsense the care and effort that useful things need. He had studied the art himself, he said, in his early years, wanting to make it his living: if he had understood Hippocrates, he could certainly have understood that. And yet he had given it up and taken to medicine for one reason only — he had found it utterly false, and, being a serious man, he would not earn his bread by fooling people. "But you have rhetoric to live on," he said, "so you follow this thing by free choice, not by necessity. All the more reason, then, to believe me about it, since I worked to master it so completely that I meant to live by it alone." I asked him how it was, then, that so many true things were foretold by it. He answered, as well as anyone could, that the force of chance, scattered through the whole order of things, brought it about. If a man opens the pages of some poet at random — a poet singing and thinking of something else entirely — a line often falls out that fits his present business wonderfully. So it was no marvel, he said, if from the soul of a man, by some higher instinct and without the soul's knowing what happens inside it, an answer should come out that chimes with the asker's business and doings — by luck, not by art.

That much you procured for me from him, or through him, and you traced into my memory what I would later search out for myself. But at the time, neither he nor my dearest Nebridius — a young man singularly good and singularly clean of heart, who laughed at the whole business of divination — could persuade me to throw it away. The authority of the authors still weighed more with me, and I had not yet found the certain proof I was looking for: proof that would show, past all doubt, that when these consulted men said true things, it was chance speaking, not the art of the star-readers.

In those years — the time when I first began to teach in the town where I was born — I had made a friend, too dear to me, my own age, sharing my studies, flowering with me in the first flower of young manhood. He had grown up with me as a boy; we had gone to school together, played together. But he was not yet my friend the way he later became — and even then, not the way true friendship is. For there is no true friendship unless you glue it together, between people who hold fast to you, with the love poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who is given to us. Still, it was something almost too sweet, ripened in the heat of shared enthusiasms. I had even bent him away from the true faith — which as a youth he had never taken in deeply or thoroughly — toward those superstitious, soul-destroying fables my mother wept over in me. With me, now, the man wandered in his mind; and my soul could not do without him. But look: you were right behind your runaways — God of vengeance and fountain of mercies at once, who turn us back to you by astonishing means — look: you took the man out of this life when he had scarcely filled one whole year of a friendship sweeter to me than every sweetness of that life of mine.

Who can count up all your praises — even those a single man has felt in his single self? What did you do then, my God? How unsearchable is the abyss of your judgments! For a long time he lay senseless in a death-sweat, burnt through with fever, and when they gave up hope for him, he was baptized — knowing nothing of it. I hardly cared. I took it for granted that his soul would keep what it had learned from me, and not whatever had been done to a body that could not feel it. It turned out very differently: he rallied; he was saved. And the moment I could talk with him — which was the moment he could talk, for I never left him, and we hung on each other far too much — I tried joking with him, expecting him to laugh with me about that baptism he had received while absent in mind and sense, though by now he had learned that he had received it. He recoiled from me as if from an enemy. With a sudden, startling freedom he told me that if I wished to stay his friend, I would stop saying such things to him. I was astonished; I was shaken; and I buried every feeling I had until he should be well again, strong enough for me to handle as I pleased. But he was snatched away from my madness, to be kept safe with you for my consolation. A few days later, while I was away, the fever came back, and he died.

At that grief my heart went black. Everything I looked at was death. My own country was a torture to me, my father's house a strange unhappiness; and everything I had shared with him became, without him, one immense torment. My eyes looked for him everywhere, and he was not given to them. I hated all places because he was not in them — because they could no longer tell me, "Look, he's coming," as they could when he was alive and only away. I had become a great question to myself. I kept asking my soul why it was sad, and why it troubled me so deeply, and it had no answer to give me. And if I said, "Hope in God," it rightly refused to obey — because the man it had lost, that dearest man, was truer and better than the phantasm it was being ordered to hope in. Only weeping was sweet to me, and tears took my friend's place among the delights of my heart.

And now, Lord, all that has passed, and time has softened my wound. May I hear from you, who are Truth — may I put the ear of my heart against your mouth — and will you tell me why weeping is sweet to the miserable? Have you, though present everywhere, flung our misery far away from you? You abide in yourself, while we are rolled through trial after trial. And yet, if we could not cry into your ears, nothing of our hope would be left at all. How is it, then, that sweet fruit is picked from life's bitterness — from mourning, weeping, sighing, complaint? Is the sweetness this, that we hope you hear? In prayer, yes, rightly so: prayer carries the longing to reach you. But in grief for a lost thing — in the sorrow that had buried me then? I had no hope he would come back to life; my tears were not begging for that. I simply grieved, and wept: I was miserable, and I had lost my joy. Or is weeping a bitter thing after all, which pleases us only out of revulsion — only in the moment we recoil from the things we used to enjoy?

But why am I saying all this? Now is no time for questions; now is the time to confess to you. I was miserable, and every soul is miserable that is tied by friendship to mortal things: it is shredded when it loses them, and only then does it feel the misery that was in it even before it lost them. That is how it was with me then. I wept with utter bitterness, and I rested in the bitterness. So miserable was I that I held that miserable life dearer than my friend himself. However much I might have wished to change it, I was less willing to lose it than to lose him — I doubt I would have given it even for him, in the way tradition tells (if it is not invention) of Orestes and Pylades, who wanted to die for each other, or die together, since to them not living together was worse than dying. In me a feeling had risen up quite contrary to that, and I could not explain it: a crushing weariness of being alive, and at the same time a fear of dying. I believe that the more I loved him, the more I hated death, which had taken him from me, and the more I feared it, as the most savage of enemies; and I imagined it would suddenly devour every human being, since it had been able to devour him. That is how it was with me — I remember. Look at my heart, my God; look inside it and see, for I do remember, O my Hope, you who wash me clean of the uncleanness of such affections, turning my eyes toward you, pulling my feet out of the snare. For I marveled that the rest of the mortals went on living, when the man I had loved as though he would never die was dead; and I marveled more that I, his other self, was alive when he was dead. Someone once called his friend "the half of my soul," and said it well. For I felt that my soul and his soul had been one soul in two bodies; and that is why living horrified me — I refused to live as a half. And that, perhaps, is why I was afraid to die: so that the man I had loved so much would not die entirely.

What madness — not to know how to love human beings as human beings! What a fool, to take the human lot with so little measure! That was what I was then. So I seethed, I sighed, I wept, I was in turmoil; there was no rest, and no counsel. For I was carrying my soul around cut open and bloodied — a soul that could not stand being carried by me — and I could find nowhere to lay it down. Not in pleasant groves; not in games and songs; not in sweet-scented places; not in elegant banquets; not in the pleasures of bedroom and bed; not, finally, in books or in poetry would it rest. Everything looked ghastly, even light itself; and whatever was not what he had been was repellent and hateful — all of it, except groaning and tears. In those alone was there a little relief; and whenever my soul was taken from them, a huge freight of misery weighed me down. To you, Lord, it should have been lifted, for you to lighten it. I knew that. But I neither would nor could — all the less because, when I thought of you, you were nothing solid or firm to me. It was not you at all: my god was an empty phantasm, my own error. If I tried to lay my burden down on it, to let it rest, it slid through the void and came crashing back down on me; and I had remained, to myself, an unhappy place, where I could not stay and from which I could not get away. For where could my heart run from my heart? Where could I run from myself? Where would I not follow myself? And yet I fled my own country. My eyes would look for him less, I thought, in places where they were not used to seeing him. And so I left the town of Thagaste and came to Carthage.

Time is not idle; it does not roll uselessly over our senses. It works strange operations in the mind. Look — the days came and went, one after another, and coming and going they slipped other hopes into me, other memories, and little by little they patched me back together out of the old kinds of pleasure. To those my grief gave way. But what followed was not other griefs; it was the causes of other griefs. For why had that grief gone into me so easily and so deep, if not because I had poured out my soul on sand, loving a man who was going to die as if he would never die? What restored me most, what remade me, was the comfort of other friends — friends with whom I loved what I loved instead of you. And that was one enormous fable, one long-drawn lie, and its adulterous friction was corrupting our minds, whose itch was in the ears. But that fable would not die for me, however many of my friends died. There were other things in friendship that took a deeper hold on the mind: to talk together and laugh together; to trade kindnesses turn by turn; to read sweet-tongued books together; to be silly together and serious together; to disagree now and then without hatred, the way a man may disagree with himself, and to find those rarest disagreements the seasoning of countless agreements; to teach one another something, or learn something from one another; to miss the absent with impatience, and to welcome them home with joy. These signs, and a thousand like them, rising from the hearts of people who love and are loved in return — spoken by the mouth, the tongue, the eyes, and countless gestures of pleasure — were the kindling that fused our souls together and made, out of many, one.

That is what we love in friends — and we love it so, that a man's conscience convicts itself if he fails to love the one who loves him, or to love back the one who loved him first, asking of the other's person nothing but the signs of his goodwill. From this comes the mourning when a friend dies: the darkness of sorrows; the heart soaked through, its sweetness turned to bitterness; and, from the lost life of the dying, the death of the living. Blessed is the one who loves you — who loves his friend in you, and his enemy for your sake. For he alone loses no one dear to him, to whom everyone is dear in the One who is never lost. And who is that but our God — the God who made heaven and earth, and who fills them, since it was by filling them that he made them? No one loses you who does not let you go. And the one who lets you go — where does he go? Where can he run, except from you at peace with him to you set against him? For where will he not find your law waiting in his own punishment? And your law is truth, and truth is you.

Turn us, God of hosts; show us your face, and we will be saved. For wherever the soul of man turns, it is nailed to sorrows unless it turns to you — nailed even when it fastens on beautiful things. And those beautiful things, outside you and outside the soul, would not exist at all unless they came from you. They rise and they set: rising, they begin, as it were, to be; they grow, toward their completion; completed, they age, and they perish. Not everything ages — but everything perishes. So when they rise and reach toward being, the faster they grow into being, the harder they hurry toward not-being. That is their law. You gave them that much, because they are pieces of a whole whose pieces do not all exist at once: by giving way and taking over, all of them together act out the whole universe of which they are pieces. Our own speech is carried out the same way, through signs that sound: there is no whole sentence unless each word passes away, once it has sounded its part, so that the next may take its place. For all of this let my soul praise you, God, creator of all — but let it not be stuck fast to these things by the glue of love, through the senses of the body. For they go where they were always going: toward not-being; and they tear the soul with pestilent longings, because the soul wants to be — and it loves to rest in the things it loves. But in them there is nowhere to rest, because they do not stay. They flee: and who can follow them with the senses of the flesh? Who can grasp them even while they are near? The sense of the flesh is slow, because it is the sense of the flesh: that is its boundary. It is enough for what it was made for; it is not enough to hold things as they run their course from their appointed start to their appointed end. For in your Word, through whom they are created, they hear their orders: "Start here; end here."

Don't be empty, my soul; don't let the ear of your heart go deaf with the racket of your own emptiness. Listen — you too. The Word himself is crying out for you to return, and there is the place of rest that cannot be disturbed, where love is not abandoned unless it abandons first. Look: these things pass away so that other things may take their place, so that this lowest order of the universe may be complete in all its parts. "But do I go anywhere?" says the Word of God. Fix your dwelling there. Whatever you have from there, my soul, place it there in trust — now at least, tired out as you are with deceptions. Entrust to the Truth whatever the truth has given you, and you will lose nothing. The rot in you will flower again; all your diseases will be healed; all in you that drains away will be formed anew, made new, bound close around you. They will not drop you where they descend, but will stand with you, and hold, before the God who stands and holds forever.

Why keep following your own flesh, turned backwards? Turn around, and let it follow you. Whatever you sense through the flesh is a part; the whole to which the parts belong, you do not know — yet the parts delight you. But if the flesh's senses were fit to take in the whole — if they had not, for your punishment, been justly confined to a part of it — you would want whatever exists in the present moment to pass away, so that the whole could please you more. When we speak, you hear us through that same sense of flesh — and you certainly do not want the syllables to stand still; you want them to fly past, so that others can come and you can hear the whole. That is how it always is, when one thing is made of many parts that do not exist all at once: all of it, could all of it be perceived, would please more than the pieces do. But better by far than all of it is he who made all of it: he is our God. And he does not pass away, because there is nothing to take his place.

If bodies please you, praise God for them and turn your love back around, onto their maker — lest in the things that please you, you displease. If souls please you, love them in God; for they too are changeable, and only fixed in him do they stand firm — otherwise they would go, and be gone. Love them in him, then, and sweep up with you to him every soul you can, and say to them: "Let us love him — let us love him! He made these things, and he is not far away. He did not make them and then leave; they are from him, and they are in him. Look where he is: he is wherever truth is savored. He is inmost in the heart itself — but the heart has strayed from him. Come back to your heart, you deserters, and hold fast to the one who made you. Stand with him, and you will stand. Rest in him, and you will be at rest. Where are you going, over such rough ground? Where are you going? The good you love is from him — and turned toward him it is good and it is sweet; but it will turn bitter, and justly so, because whatever is from him is loved unjustly if he is deserted for its sake. What do you want, walking on and on down these hard and weary roads? There is no rest where you are seeking it. Seek what you seek — but it is not where you are seeking it. You seek a happy life in the country of death, and it is not there. How can there be a happy life where there is no life at all?

"But our true Life came down here and carried our death away, and killed it out of the abundance of his own life. And he thundered, calling us to return from here to him — back into that secret place from which he first came forth to us: into the Virgin's womb itself, where the human creature was wedded to him, mortal flesh, that it might not be mortal forever; and from there, like a bridegroom coming out of his chamber, he exulted like a champion to run his race. He did not linger — he ran, shouting by his words, his deeds, his death, his life, his descent, his ascent, shouting to us to return to him. And he withdrew from our eyes, so that we would return into our own hearts and find him there. He went away — and look: he is here. He would not stay long with us, and he has not left us. He went back to the place he never departed from, because the world was made through him; and he was in this world, and he came into this world to save sinners. To him my soul confesses, and he heals it, because it sinned against him. You sons of men, how long will you be so heavy of heart? Even now, after Life itself has come down to you, will you not climb up and live? But where can you climb, when you are already high, with your mouths set against the heavens? Come down, so that you can climb — climb, this time, to God. For you fell when you climbed against him." Tell them this, my soul, and let them weep in the valley of weeping — and so carry them up with you to God; for it is by his Spirit that you say this to them, if you say it burning with the fire of love.

None of this did I know then. I loved the lower beauties, and I was sinking toward the bottom, and I would say to my friends: "Do we love anything except the beautiful? Then what is the beautiful? And what is beauty? What is it in the things we love that pulls us and binds us to them? Unless there were some grace in them, some form, they could not possibly draw us." And I looked, and I noticed that in bodies themselves there is one beauty that comes of being a kind of whole, and another that comes of fitting — of answering well to something else, as a part of the body answers to its whole body, or a shoe to a foot, and so on. This thought welled up in my mind from the bottom of my heart, and I wrote some books — "On the Beautiful and the Fitting," I think — two of them, or three. You know, God; it has slipped from me. I no longer have them; they wandered away from me, I don't know how.

But what was it, Lord my God, that moved me to dedicate those books to Hierius, an orator of the city of Rome? I did not know him by sight. I loved the man for his reputation for learning, which was brilliant, and for a few sayings of his I had heard and liked. But he pleased me more because he pleased others: people praised him to the skies, amazed that a Syrian, schooled first in Greek eloquence, should afterward have turned into a marvelous speaker of Latin too, and one supremely learned in everything that belongs to the pursuit of wisdom. A man is praised, and, sight unseen, he is loved. Does the love enter the hearer's heart from the mouth of the one praising? No. One lover kindles another. That is why a man who is praised gets loved: because we believe the praise comes from an undeceiving heart — that is, that the one praising already loves him.

That is how I loved men then: on the judgment of men, not on yours, my God, in which no one is deceived. Still — why not love him the way one loves a famous charioteer, or a beast-fighter adored by the crowds, instead of so very differently, so seriously — exactly the way I wanted to be praised myself? For I would not have wanted to be praised and loved the way actors are — though I myself praised and loved actors. I would sooner have been unknown than known like that; sooner hated than loved like that. Where does one soul store the weights of so many different and contrary loves? Why do I love in another man what — since we are equally men — I would detest and throw off from myself, if I did not hate it? A good horse may be loved by a man who would not choose to be that horse even if he could; but you cannot say the same of an actor, who shares our nature. Do I then love in a man what I would hate to be, though I am a man? Man himself is a vast deep. You, Lord, keep the count of his very hairs, and not one of them is lost in you; and yet the hairs of his head are easier to number than his feelings — than the movements of his heart.

That orator was of the kind I loved in the way of wanting to be him. And I strayed, swollen with conceit, carried around by every wind — and all the while, in deepest secret, you were steering me. And how do I know — how can I confess it to you as a certainty — that I loved him more in the love of his praisers than for the things they praised? Because if those same men, instead of praising him, had torn him down — if they had reported the very same facts about him with scorn and contempt — I would never have caught fire for him, never been stirred. And yet the facts would have been no different; the man himself no different; only the feeling of the tellers. Look where the strengthless soul lies, when it is not yet fastened to the solidity of truth: as the gusts of tongues blow out of the chests of the opinionated, the soul is carried and turned, twisted and twisted back; the light clouds over, and it cannot make out the truth. And look — the truth is right in front of us. To me, back then, it was a very great matter that my style and my studies should become known to that man. If he approved them, I would blaze all the hotter; if he disapproved, my heart — hollow, void of your solidity — would have taken the wound. And yet that "beautiful and fitting" I had written to him about, I liked turning over in my mind, gazing on it and admiring it, with no one to praise it with me.

But I did not yet see the hinge on which this great question turns: your craftsmanship, Almighty — you who alone do wonders. My mind moved among bodily forms. The "beautiful" I defined as what pleases in itself; the "fitting" as what pleases by suiting something else; and I shored up the distinction with examples drawn from bodies. Then I turned to the nature of the mind — and the false notion I held of spiritual things would not let me see what was true. The sheer force of the truth kept beating against my eyes, and I kept turning my quivering mind away from bodiless reality toward outlines and colors and swollen masses; and since I could not see such things in the mind, I concluded that I could not see my mind. And since in virtue I loved peace, and in vice I hated discord, I noted in the one a unity, in the other a kind of division; and it seemed to me that in that unity lay the rational mind and the very nature of truth and of the highest good, while in that division — this was my misery — there was some substance of irrational life, and the nature of a highest evil: not merely a substance, but genuinely a life, and yet not from you, my God, from whom all things are. The first I called a Monad — a mind, as it were, without any sex; the second a Dyad: anger in crimes of violence, lust in crimes of the flesh. I did not know what I was saying. For I had not known, and had not learned, that evil is not a substance at all — and that our own mind is not the highest and unchangeable good.

For as crimes of violence arise when the surge of the soul from which action springs is corrupted and hurls itself forward, insolent and turbid; and as crimes of the flesh arise when the soul's appetite for drinking in bodily pleasures runs unbridled: just so do errors and false opinions poison a life when the reasoning mind itself is corrupt. And so it was then in me — a mind that did not know it must be lit by another light in order to share in the truth, since it is not itself the nature of truth. For you will light my lamp, Lord; my God, you will turn my darkness to light; and from your fullness we have all received. For you are the true light, which gives light to every man who comes into this world; and in you there is no changing — not even the shadow thrown by turning.

I strained toward you, and was pushed back from you so that I might taste death — for you resist the proud. And what is prouder than to claim, with unbelievable madness, that I was by nature what you are? I was changeable, and I knew it — plainly, since the very fact that I wanted to become wise meant I wanted to go from worse to better. Yet I preferred to imagine even you changeable, rather than admit that I was not what you are. So you pushed me back; you set yourself against my stiff, wind-filled neck. And I went on imagining bodily shapes; flesh myself, I put flesh on trial; a wind that walks away and does not come back, I did not return to you, but wandered on and on, toward things that have no being at all — not in you, not in me, not in the body. None of it was created for me by your truth; all of it was invented by my vanity out of body. And I used to say to your faithful little ones, my fellow citizens — from whom, without knowing it, I was living in exile — I used to say to them, glib and fatuous: "Why does the soul go wrong, if God made it?" But I did not want anyone to say to me, "Why does God go wrong, then?" And I argued that your unchangeable substance erred under compulsion, sooner than confess that my changeable substance had swerved of its own free will, and that its erring now was punishment.

I was perhaps twenty-six or twenty-seven years old when I wrote those volumes — turning over inside me bodily fictions that drummed at the ears of my heart. And I was straining those ears, sweet Truth, for your inward melody, thinking on the beautiful and the fitting, longing to stand still and hear you and to rejoice with joy at the voice of the Bridegroom — and I could not. The voices of my own error dragged me outward, and under the weight of my own pride I kept sinking toward the lowest place. You did not give joy and gladness to my hearing; and the bones did not exult, because they had not been humbled.

When I was about twenty, a certain work of Aristotle fell into my hands. They call it the Ten Categories, and at the bare name of it I would stand open-mouthed, as before something great and divine, whenever my rhetoric master at Carthage, and others reckoned learned, pronounced it with their cheeks bursting with pride. And what good did it do me that I read it alone, and understood it? I compared notes with others, who said that even with the most erudite teachers — teachers who did not just lecture on it, but drew diagram after diagram in the sand — they had barely understood it; and they could tell me nothing about it that I had not already gathered reading it by myself. The book seemed to me to speak plainly enough about substances, such as "a man," and about what is in them: the figure of a man, what it is like; his stature, how many feet; his kinship, whose brother he is; where he is placed; when he was born; whether he stands or sits; whether he is shod or armed; whether he is doing something or having something done to him — and all the innumerable things that fall under those nine categories, of which I have set down a few samples, or under the chief category, substance itself.

What good was this to me — when in fact it did me harm? For, supposing that those ten categories covered absolutely everything that is, I tried to understand even you that way, my God — you, wonderfully simple, wonderfully unchanging — as though you too were the subject in which your greatness or your beauty resided, existing in you as they exist in a body. But your greatness and your beauty are you yourself; whereas a body is not great or beautiful simply by being a body — were it less great and less beautiful, it would be a body still. What I was thinking about you was falsehood, not truth: the fictions of my own misery, not the firm ground of your blessedness. For you had commanded it, and so it was being done in me: the earth was bearing me briars and thorns, and I was reaching my bread by the sweat of my face.

And what good did it do me that I read on my own, and understood, every book I could lay hands on of the arts they call liberal — I, at that time the vile slave of vile desires? I delighted in the books, and had no idea where whatever in them was true and certain came from. For I had my back to the light and my face to the things the light fell on; and so my face, by which I saw the lit things, caught no light itself. Whatever was written on rhetoric or on logic, on the measuring of figures, on music, on numbers, I understood without much difficulty, without any man to teach me — you know it, Lord my God, because quickness of understanding and sharpness of analysis are your gift. But I offered you no sacrifice from it. So it worked not for my use but rather for my ruin, since I fought to keep so good a part of my inheritance in my own power, and did not keep my strength for you, but set out from you into a far country, to squander my substance there on whoring passions. For what good was a good thing to me, when I did not use it well? I never realized how hard those arts are — hard even for the studious and the gifted — until I tried to explain them to the studious and the gifted, and found that the most brilliant of them was simply the one who was not too slow in following me.

But what good was any of it to me, while I supposed that you, Lord God of truth, were a vast and luminous body, and I a broken-off piece of that body? Perversity past all measure! But that is what I was. And I am not ashamed now, my God, to confess to you your mercies over me, and to call upon you — I who then was not ashamed to profess my blasphemies in front of men, and to bark at you. What use to me, then, was a mind so nimble in those sciences — all those knotted volumes untied with no help from any human teacher — when in the teaching of true devotion I was going foully, sacrilegiously wrong? And what harm was a far slower mind to your little ones, who never wandered far from you — who could grow their feathers in safety in the nest of your Church, and feed the wings of love on the food of a sound faith? O Lord our God, let us hope in the shelter of your wings: protect us, and carry us. You will carry us — you will carry us when we are small, and when our hair is white you will carry us still; for when our strength is you, it is strength, and when it is our own, it is weakness. Our good lives always with you, and because we have turned away from it, we have gone wrong. Let us turn back now, Lord, so that we are not overturned — because our good lives with you, lacking nothing; and that good is you yourself. And we need not be afraid that there is no place to come back to, just because we fell out of it: in our absence, our house does not fall down — our house, which is your eternity.

Accept the sacrifice of my confessions from the hand of my tongue — you formed that tongue, and you stirred it up to confess your name. Heal all my bones, and let them say: Lord, who is like you? A man who confesses to you is not telling you anything new about himself; a closed heart does not shut out your eye, and the hardness of a human heart cannot push back your hand. You melt it whenever you choose, in mercy or in vengeance, and nothing can hide from your heat. Let my soul praise you, so that it may love you; let it confess your mercies to you, so that it may praise you. Your whole creation never stops praising you, never falls silent: every human spirit turns its voice toward you, and every animal and lifeless thing praises you through the mouths of those who contemplate them — so that our souls may rouse themselves out of weariness and rise toward you, leaning on the things you have made and passing beyond them to you, who made them so wonderfully. And there is refreshment there, and real strength.

Let the restless and the wicked run; let them flee from you. You see them anyway; you divide the shadows. And look — the whole, with them inside it, is beautiful, though they themselves are ugly. What harm have they done you? How have they disgraced your rule, which is just and whole from the heavens down to the lowest things of earth? Where did they run, when they ran from your face? Where will you fail to find them? They ran so they would not see you seeing them — ran blind, and blundered into you, because you abandon nothing you have made. The unjust blundered into you and were justly hurt: pulling away from your gentleness, striking against your straightness, falling on their own jaggedness. They do not know, evidently, that you are everywhere, that no place contains you, that you alone stay near even to those who put themselves far away. Then let them turn and look for you. You have not abandoned your creation the way they abandoned their Creator. Let them turn — and look, there you are, in their heart, in the heart of everyone who confesses to you, who throws himself on you and weeps into your breast after all his hard roads. And you gently wipe away the tears, and they weep the more, and are glad in the weeping — because it is you, Lord, not some human being of flesh and blood, but you, Lord, their maker, who remake them and console them. And where was I, when I was looking for you? You were right in front of me; but I had walked away — even from myself. I could not find myself. How much less you.

Let me lay open before my God my twenty-ninth year. A Manichee bishop named Faustus had just arrived in Carthage — a great snare of the devil, and many people were tangled in him, caught by the lure of his smooth talk. I admired the talk too, but I could tell it apart from the truth of the things I was hungry to learn: I cared less for the serving-dish of his rhetoric than for the knowledge this Faustus, so celebrated among them, was supposed to set in front of me. His reputation had reached me ahead of him: superbly trained in every honorable study, an expert in the liberal arts. And since I had read a good deal of the philosophers and kept it in memory, I compared some of their claims with the endless fables of the Manichees, and the philosophers seemed to me more probable — men with strength enough to take the measure of this world, though they never found its Lord. Because you are great, Lord, and you look kindly on the lowly, but the proud you know only from far off. You come near to the broken-hearted alone; the proud do not find you — not even if their exacting skill could count the stars and the grains of sand, survey the fields of the sky, and trace out the paths of the planets.

With the mind and the intelligence you gave them, they investigate these things, and they have found out a great deal. They predicted eclipses of the sun and the moon years in advance — the day, the hour, how much of the light would go — and the arithmetic did not fail them: it happened exactly as they foretold. They wrote down the rules they discovered, and the rules are read to this day, and from them others still predict the year, the month, the day, the hour, and what fraction of its light the moon or the sun is going to lose — and it goes dark on schedule. People who do not know the art marvel and are dumbfounded; people who know it exult and are puffed up. In their godless pride they draw back from you, and your light fails inside them; and they can see an eclipse of the sun coming years ahead, but their own eclipse, happening now, they cannot see. Because they never ask, reverently, where the intelligence came from that they use to investigate all this. And when they do discover that you made them, they do not hand themselves over to you, so that you can preserve what you made; they do not slaughter for you what they have made of themselves. They do not kill their soaring pretensions, like birds of the air; or their diving curiosities, like fish of the sea that wander the hidden paths of the deep; or their appetites, like beasts of the field — so that you, God, a devouring fire, could burn up their dead preoccupations and re-create the men themselves for immortality.

But they did not know the way: your Word, through whom you made the things they count, and the men who do the counting, and the senses by which they perceive what they count, and the mind they count with. And of your wisdom there is no counting. The Only-begotten himself was made wisdom for us, and righteousness, and sanctification; he was counted as one of us, and he paid his tax to Caesar. They did not know this way — the way down from themselves to him, and through him up to him. They did not know it; they thought themselves high and shining among the stars, and look, they crashed to the earth, and their foolish heart went dark. They say many true things about the creation, but the Truth, the master craftsman of creation, they do not seek reverently, and so they do not find him.
